summary: Describes how to use TLS with mutual X.509 authentication to secure NETCONF. It is a revision of RFC 5539 and documents operational experience.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains how a NETCONF client and server protect a device-management session with TLS. Both sides authenticate with certificates before they exchange NETCONF messages.

questions: what port does netconf over tls use
how does netconf derive a username from a certificate
subtitle: How NETCONF management sessions use TLS and mutual X.509 certificates to authenticate both peers.

tldr.problem: NETCONF reads and changes device configuration, so its connection needs confidentiality, integrity, reliable delivery and authentication of both peers.
tldr.mechanism: The NETCONF client opens TLS on TCP port 6513. Both peers validate X.509 certificates, and the server maps the client's certificate to a NETCONF username before the session begins.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7589 obsoletes RFC 5539 and documents NETCONF 1.1 framing and certificate-to-username mapping. RFC 9918 later updated it.

today: RFC 7589 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2015. It obsoletes RFC 5539 and has been updated by RFC 9918.

sections.title: Why NETCONF Uses Mutual TLS
sections.content:
NETCONF manages network-device configuration and state over a persistent connection. The connection needs confidentiality, integrity, peer authentication and reliable, sequenced delivery. RFC 7589 defines how to carry NETCONF messages over Transport Layer Security (TLS).

Implementations MUST support mutual certificate-based authentication. The server verifies the identity of the client that may change management data, and the client verifies the server it intends to manage. Identity checks finish before the NETCONF session begins.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides must verify who they are communicating with before a management session starts. TLS protects the NETCONF messages exchanged over the connection.

sections.title: Opening and Closing a Session
sections.content:
The NETCONF client acts as the TLS client and opens the connection. The server listens on TCP port 6513. The client begins the TLS handshake with ClientHello, and the server MUST request the client's certificate with CertificateRequest.

After TLS finishes and both identities are verified, the peers may exchange NETCONF messages. The client closes the session with the <close-session> operation. The server responds and then closes the TLS session.
sections.plainLanguage: The client connects to the server's TCP port 6513 and starts a TLS handshake. Both identities are checked before either peer sends the NETCONF hello message.

sections.title: Framing NETCONF Messages
sections.content:
TLS records do not necessarily line up with NETCONF message boundaries: one record can contain several messages, or one message can span several records. NETCONF therefore uses its own framing while sending messages as TLS application data.

The initial <hello> message MUST end with ]]>]]>. If both peers advertise the :base:1.1 capability, they use chunked framing for the rest of the session. Otherwise, they use the older end-of-message framing defined in RFC 6242.
sections.plainLanguage: A TLS record does not always contain exactly one NETCONF message. The peers use an end marker for the hello, then use chunked framing if both advertise the NETCONF 1.1 capability.

sections.title: Validating Certificates and Identities
sections.content:
Both peers MUST validate the other peer's X.509 certificate path under RFC 5280. A certificate may also be accepted if it matches a certificate obtained through another trusted method, such as a locally configured fingerprint. If neither check succeeds, the connection MUST end.

The client MUST check the server identity using RFC 6125. The server MUST verify the client's identity before starting the NETCONF session. The certificate identity used by the client is converted into a NETCONF username by a server-configured, ordered mapping list.
sections.plainLanguage: Each peer checks that the other peer's certificate is trusted and matches the expected identity. The server must complete the client check before opening the NETCONF session.

sections.title: Mapping a Certificate to a Username
sections.content:
The server keeps an ordered list of certificate mappings. Each entry contains a certificate fingerprint, a mapping type and optional auxiliary data. An entry matches the client's certificate or a trusted CA certificate in its certificate chain.

The mapping type can use a configured username, a subjectAltName email-style name, DNS name or IP address, the first supported subjectAltName value, or the certificate CommonName. CommonName mapping is deprecated in favor of subjectAltName methods. If an entry cannot produce a valid NETCONF username, the server tries later entries; if none succeeds, it MUST terminate TLS.

The selected username is passed unchanged to the NETCONF layer, where the server knows its permissions.
sections.plainLanguage: The server checks configured certificate mappings in order and uses the first one that produces a valid NETCONF username. If no entry works, it ends the connection.

sections.title: Access Control and Framing Risks
sections.content:
NETCONF can expose or change sensitive configuration, including usernames and security keys. Access should be limited to authorized users and systems. If a deployment trusts a CA certificate for client access, the RFC recommends that the CA issue certificates only for NETCONF access; otherwise certificates issued for unrelated uses may also be accepted.

The end marker ]]>]]> can appear in well-formed XML, contrary to an assumption in RFC 5539. RFC 7589 retains it for the initial hello for compatibility, but switches to chunked framing after hello when both peers support :base:1.1 to avoid injection attacks.

The RFC requires TLS 1.2 support and refers to its cipher-suite recommendations. It does not support third-party authentication through a backend AAA server; it points to the SSH transport when that form of authentication is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Only authorized users should reach NETCONF because it can change device settings. The initial message framing remains for compatibility, but supported peers switch to chunked framing for later messages.
